Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall let his performance do all the talking at Hill Dickinson Stadium on Friday night.

The Everton midfielder endured a disappointing start to his matchday preparations just hours earlier after learning that, despite his impressive performances in recent weeks, he had been overlooked by England manager Thomas Tuchel for this month's Nations League fixtures.

It was a setback for the 28-year-old, who was tipped to earn a place in Tuchel's latest squad but was ultimately left out, with Borussia Dortmund teenager Jobe Bellingham selected instead.

By the end of the night, though, Dewsbury-Hall had every reason to smile.

The midfielder was celebrating alongside the Everton faithful after his thunderous strike helped the Blues to a comeback victory over Coventry City , securing an impressive 3-1 win and lifting them to fifth in the Premier League table.

"It was a disappointing morning, I'm not going to lie. It's a massive dream of mine to play for my country. I know I was close," Dewsbury-Hall told Sky Sports after Everton made it back-to-back Premier League wins.

"[I'm] sad, yeah, but really proud of myself and how I have reacted. All I can keep doing is putting in good performances and hopefully one day I get the nod, because I'm never going to give up."

Dewsbury-Hall joined Everton from Chelsea in August 2025

The wait until the next international break in March will undoubtedly feel like an eternity for Dewsbury-Hall.

But the Everton midfielder is no stranger to taking the long road to success, having experienced plenty of setbacks and detours throughout his career.

He did not make his Premier League debut for boyhood club Leicester City until the age of 22, having spent previous seasons gaining valuable experience out on loan in the English Football League with Luton Town and Blackpool.

Even when his opportunity to establish himself in the Foxes' first team finally arrived, it came during a turbulent period for the club, which ultimately ended in relegation from the Premier League at the end of the following season.

After playing a starring role in Leicester's Championship-winning campaign under Enzo Maresca, the midfielder soon followed the Italian to Chelsea in a deal worth £30m.

However, Dewsbury-Hall struggled for regular game time during his only season at Chelsea , featuring mainly in cup competitions with limited opportunities in the Premier League.

It was only after his move to Everton last summer, at the age of 26, that he appeared to have finally found the right environment to reignite his career and showcase the qualities that made him once such a highly regarded attacking midfielder.

Since the start of last season, Dewsbury-Hall has scored 11 goals for Everton in the Premier League and provided seven assists.

"I'm really, really enjoying it," said Dewsbury-Hall. "I've got a really good hybrid role in this team, where the gaffer is giving me the freedom to pop up all over the pitch."

Tuchel said on Friday afternoon that Dewsbury-Hall had been "very close" to earning a place in his squad, having enjoyed "a very good season" with Everton so far.

"I've got the mentality," added Dewsbury-Hall. "I'll keep pushing and pushing and see what happens."

Thierno Barry has scored 10 goals for Everton across all competitions this season

It was not just Dewsbury-Hall who caught the eye against Coventry , with Thierno Barry scoring twice in the space of five minutes at the start of the second half to help Everton come from behind.

By taking his tally for the season into double figures across all competitions, the 24-year-old - who struggled for both form and confidence after joining the Blues from Spanish side Villarreal last summer - has already surpassed the eight goals he scored last season.

Not only is the French forward lighting up Hill Dickinson Stadium with his goals, he is also setting the place alight with his dance moves.

Barry has made a habit of celebrating every goal with some kind of viral dance move - and that was certainly the case on Friday night.

"I was on TikTok yesterday and I saw an NFL guy do the celebration. I said to Tyrique [George] that if we scored tomorrow, we would do the dance like that, but I think he was shy to do it, so I did the dance alone," Barry told Match of the Day.

The former Basel and Villarreal frontman is also drawing inspiration from Haaland as he looks to maintain his impressive goalscoring form.

The Manchester City forward is the only Premier League player with more goals (14) in all competitions than the 10 Barry has managed this campaign for David Moyes' side.

"I'm very happy because I'm a fan of him," said Barry. "I watch a lot of videos of him and try and do the things he does. If I can play with him until the end to get the Golden Boot, I will try."

Earlier in the night, Moyes equaled Harry Catterick's record for the most games as Everton manager - with 592 matches each.

The late Catterick managed the Toffees from 1961 to 1973.

"I am proud," Moyes said in Everton 's match programme.

"The thought of being the Everton manager who has managed the most games is something I'm very proud of.

" Everton has been huge for me and my family. My son David has gone everywhere and my father has lived it with us as well, watching it all.

"That's so important. What is also so important is that I'll always try to do the right thing for Everton Football Club."

Cornell University is an Ivy League institution in upstate New York

Cornell University's academic staff have passed a vote of no confidence over its leadership's handling of what staff call a "crisis of sexual assault" after a former student alleged she was gang raped while attending.

The woman, known anonymously as Jane Doe, is suing her former university and the fraternity over an alleged incident involving several men at the Chi Phi fraternity house in October 2024.

All seven of the accused have denied wrongdoing when contacted by the BBC's US partner CBS. None has been charged with a crime.

Friday's no-confidence vote passed by 75 votes to 50. It is largely symbolic because the faculty senate does not have the power to remove leaders.

The resolution states that the faculty senate, which represents academic staff, "has no confidence in the ability of the central administration to effectively address the ongoing crisis of sexual assault at Cornell University".

It did not make any specific recommendations or suggest what administrators did wrong in response to the accusation.

It is a rebuke of university leaders including President Michael Kotlikoff, whom Doe has accused of asking why she waited several weeks to report the incident.

The Ivy League institution in upstate New York has said her account of Kotlikoff's reaction is "incorrect".

Doe's lawyer, Thomas Giuffra, responded to the vote's outcome in a statement, saying: "We recently learned that Cornell's Faculty Senate made a finding of no confidence in the Central Administration's ability to address the longstanding crisis of sexual assault at Cornell.

"We believe that the Faculty Senate did not reach this decision lightly and considered all available information."

Giuffra added: "We are hopeful that this will be yet another step forward to educate and support the Cornell community by addressing the longstanding scourge of sexual assault on campus."

The board of trustees, which does have the power to fire Kotlikoff, said in a statement that it "remains confident" that he and his administration "are the right leaders to thoughtfully and comprehensively address the serious problem of sexual assault on our campus".

Trustees board chairwoman Anne Meinig Smalling, added: "This confidence is rooted not only in the administration's actions to date and plans moving forward, but also in its track record of navigating complex problems."

She also said that the vote of no confidence "reflects the deep anger across our campus and sends a clear signal that what happened to Jane Doe is unacceptable".

Backlash against Cornell has been intense since Doe filed her lawsuit in September. She reported the alleged assault to campus police after it happened but the local prosecutor declined to bring charges at the time.

Cornell, after initially defending its disciplinary measures, has acknowledged it fell short in its handling of her case and has hired a former attorney general to conduct an independent review of the case. It also recently announced a series of measures due assault, including cancelling fraternity parties.

New York state prosecutors, led by Attorney General Letitia James, are carrying out their own investigation to decide if criminal charges are warranted.

Earlier this week, New York Governor Kathy Hochul announced that state police would investigate any future sexual offence complaints at the university.

In the aftermath of the Republican Party's sweeping defeat in Tuesday's midterm elections, Donald Trump said he would be willing to work with the newly ascendent Democrats in Congress.

On Friday, however, he elevated Stephen Miller, his bare-knuckled political operative and longtime adviser, to replace Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff.

Far from an olive branch to Congress, Miller's promotion could be a sign that the president is girding for political battle by installing a partisan firebrand in the top White House job.

"The mission now is more clear than ever: Fight with all of our soul to support our president and defend this magnificent republic," Miller posted on X, adding that he was "honored beyond words" to be Trump's pick for the job.

One of the most powerful positions in Washington, the chief of staff is gatekeeper to the president, agenda-setter in the White House and chief negotiator with Congress and other outside political interests.

"Stephen Miller's been with me since the beginning," Trump said in comments to reporters after announcing the move on his Truth Social website. "He gets it."

Watch: Trump says he appointed Stephen Miller ‘to make a change’

Miller is best known for being the driving force behind the Trump administration's aggressive immigration enforcement policies, which has included ramping up funding for enforcement operations across the US.

He made headlines when he called Alex Pretti, who was shot and killed by federal immigration officials during a massive deportation operation in Minneapolis, a "domestic terrorist" and an "assassin". He would later walk back those words, saying federal agents "may not have been following" proper protocol.

He has also reportedly played a leading role in the US military operations in Venezuela and against suspected drug trafficking operations in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific, which critics have condemned as extra-judicial killings.

Miller joined Trump's political operation early in his 2016 presidential bid as a strategist and incendiary warm-up speaker at his raucous campaign rallies.

He was one of the few senior White House staffers to persevere through the entirety of his first term. He stayed loyal to Trump during his political exile following attempts to overturn his ballot-box defeat in 2020 failed. He then returned in the influential role of deputy chief of staff for policy in Trump's second term.

Wiles, who co-managed the president's successful 2024 re-election campaign, developed a reputation as a cool professional who avoided the White House staffing upheavals, dramatic policy reversals and personality clashes that typified Trump's first presidential term.

The president, however, began souring on Wiles in recent months, as his political standing in the US declined, culminating in Tuesday's electoral rout. He also reportedly chafed at news stories indicating that those in Wiles' orbit were landing lucrative consulting jobs through their connections to the president.

Trump names Stephen Miller as new White House chief of staff

'Trump's psyche': The aide driving president's most controversial policies

What has Stephen Miller’s role been in Trump’s second term?

While Trump praised Miller's effectiveness as a manager on Friday, working with Congress could prove to be a challenge.

It is difficult to overstate how disliked Miller is by most Democrats – and some Republicans.

"Stephen Miller is a dangerous xenophobe and reckless extremist who has American blood on his hands," Democratic House leader Hakeem Jeffries wrote on X. "His presence in government should be eradicated like a malignant tumor."

Earlier this year, Miller posted on social media that James Talarico, who had just secured the Democratic nomination to run for Senate in Texas, was "their first transgender Senate candidate".

The Democratic Party offered a terse, obscenity laced reply, telling Miller to shut up.

Now Miller will have to negotiate with a US Senate that includes a newly elected Talarico as one of its rising stars, after an election in which polls found that 58% of voters believe the administration's immigration enforcement actions had "gone too far" and Hispanics decisively turned against Republican candidates.

On Wednesday, in a social media post attempting to explain the Republican midterm defeats, Vice-President JD Vance - who is an early frontrunner for the Republican 2028 presidential nomination - wrote that he was "open to the idea that we should change enforcement - by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labour, for instance".

That now seems less likely with an immigration hardline taking the White House helm.

Thom Tillis, the North Carolina Republican senator who is retiring at the end of the year, has been particularly vocal in condemning Miller. He has called him "incompetent" and "the architect of some of the dumbest proposals from the Trump White House".

Other Republicans, however, have sung his praises.

"Stephen Miller has been a true conservative warrior since his days as a Senate staffer, a staunch defender of law and order against illegal invasions and leftist lawlessness, and a steadfast fighter for President Trump for over a decade," Utah Senator Mike Lee posted on X after Trump's announcement.

At a time when congressional Democrats are promising to launch new investigations and oversight into the Trump administration, it appears that a "warrior" and a "fighter" is the kind of person the president wants to have running his White House.

Coventry boss Frank Lampard questioned why his side were not given a penalty after a trio of decisions went against them in defeat at Everton .

Thierno Barry's double and Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall's late goal helped the hosts come from behind to win 3-1 on Friday .

Yann Gboho gave Coventry the lead after the break, yet the visitors felt they should have had a first-half spot-kick.

James Tarkowski tugged Caleb Yirenkyi's hair while jumping for a ball, with referee Stuart Attwell dismissing the Sky Blues' claims.

The rules have been relaxed around hair pulling this season and it does not automatically mean a foul or a red card, with excessive force and intent also being taken into consideration - but former Everton boss Lampard believes the officials got it wrong.

He said: "They're saying it's not enough of a pull and I think it's a hard area to be in. What is a hair pull? You've decided it is but it's not enough.

"I have looked at them, sometimes with emotions in the moment you can't be clear on the sidelines.

"I think the rules are fine. It's not a red card. I kind of get that because I think in a game of football there's a lot of stuff happens that's not absolutely dramatic.

"You know they can happen but I think if the the rule remains that it's a foul so I felt it was a foul."

Lampard also felt Taiwo Awoniyi was fouled by Vitalii Mykolenko before Coventry went ahead, although replays showed it was outside the box, and Barry handled the ball before his second goal - although video assistant referee (VAR) Timothy Wood ruled it was not a handball offence.

"Taiwo for me on the line of the box is a penalty. You've got to give the foul in real time anyway, the ref did let it go, and I felt it was a penalty," Lampard added, with defeat leaving Coventry 16th in the Premier League.

"The Barry one is handball, I've heard they are saying it didn't touch his hand but I've seen an angle where he has flicked it in with the final touch. VAR is there for that.

"I can't sit here and say I know everything and they should give all three of them, if one or two of them don't go our way, but they would clearly change the game."

Everton boss David Moyes denied Barry handled the ball and also felt the hair pulling rule needs addressing.

After his team moved fifth, the Scot said: "We've had plenty [of decisions] which have gone against us. It certainly doesn't hit his hand.

"The hair pull rule has changed so it would be a booking if it was but I still think it's ridiculous that rule is in the game. I can't understand why they don't fix this completely because I don't see it as a good rule at all."

Frank Lampard post-match interview - Everton v Coventry

Three big VAR calls, and they all went against Coventry . Lampard must have walked under a ladder earlier today.

There is a strong argument that the Sky Blues should have been awarded a penalty for the Tarkowski hair pull

The law was relaxed at the start of this season to say not all hair pulling should be a red card, after three players were sent off last season.

The idea is that not all contact with the hair should be an offence, and it needs to be an act with excessive force for a player to be sent off.

But, for a penalty, the actions of Tarkowski only need to be a foul, not violent conduct. If accidental, it should not be a spot-kick.

Did the Wood, the VAR, concentrate too much on a possible handball by Tarkowski within the move?

It looked like there was a movement of Tarkowski's arm to pull the hair which should have led to a VAR intervention. Coventry probably should have received a penalty.

Then early in the second half came a possible penalty as Mykolenko clipped Awoniyi.

The camera positioned level with the edge of the penalty area did seem to show the contact was outside the area, and the VAR cannot intervene to award a free-kick.

It might have been a soft VAR intervention even if the potential foul was inside the box.

Perhaps most controversially was Barry's second goal, with the ball appearing to touch the striker's arm before it went into the goal.

We have seen this kind of situation a few times this season, most notably when Nottingham Forest had a goal against Tottenham disallowed.

This time, the VAR decided he did not have the necessary conclusive proof to be sure the ball touched the hand.

Yet it does seem like there is a change of direction after Barry's hand touches the ball, and that was the reason it goes into the goal. It looked like handball should have been given on video review although others might argue that ruling it out would have been too forensic.

Three decisions, and Coventry can feel aggrieved about two of them.

Pyre's protagonists are Bubu and Aama – local terms for grandfather and grandmother

A film about the tender love and quiet loneliness of an elderly couple, which took two years to reach cinemas after it was completed, is wowing critics and audiences across India.

The 111-minute Pyre, directed by television journalist-turned-filmmaker Vinod Kapri, also explores the pressing issue of outmigration which has left hundreds of picturesque Himalayan hamlets abandoned and turned them into ghost villages. It further reflects on the impact of climate change, which has made the region's weather increasingly harsh.

On social media, many Indians have shared videos showing audiences leaving theatres with tears in their eyes. Others have posted that they have not been so moved by a film in a long time.

The film's lead actors, ordinary villagers who had never faced a camera before, have also won praise from some of Bollywood's most respected figures, including Naseeruddin Shah and Anupam Kher.

Pyre's protagonists - Padam Singh (played by Kapri's uncle, Padam Singh) and Tulsi (played by Heera Devi) - are Bubu and Aama, local terms for grandfather and grandmother. The couple live in a small home in the mountains of the northern state of Uttarakhand .

It's a place where age is measured against momentous events. Singh was born two years before the outbreak of World War II. Tulsi was born in the year atomic bombs were dropped on Japan.

There are no roads and no electricity. Whenever the couple need help – which is often as Tulsi frequently has to be carried to hospital – Padam Singh uses a traditional long-horn instrument to summon neighbours. In return for their kindness, he pays them with goats.

For Padam Singh and Tulsi, bickering is their love language

"There's nothing here – just mountains," as one character puts it. So the young leave in search of greener pastures, and those who depart this beautiful, but blighted, land rarely return.

Kapri says his film remains focused on the "soulful love story of the ageing couple in their last days".

"They have shared a life together for 65 years and, for the last 28 years, they've been waiting for their son, Hariya, who's gone to Mumbai in search of work, to come back," Kapri tells the BBC. "It's a story of companionship, of loneliness and of waiting."

Their wait takes on a new urgency when suddenly, after all these years, a letter arrives from Hariya setting a date for his visit.

As Padam Singh and Tulsi count down the days, the handful of villagers around them leave one by one, until the couple find themselves alone in the vast mountain landscape.

"You and Tulsi should also leave as soon as possible. Otherwise, you won't even have four people to carry your body down the mountain to the funeral pyre when you or Tulsi die," one departing villager advises Padam Singh. "Or die before we leave," he adds in jest.

With no one left to call for help, Padam Singh builds two funeral pyres side by side right outside his door – one for his wife and one for himself.

"How will I carry you down the mountain if you die?" he tells Tulsi when she questions the decision.

Padam Singh has to use a traditional long horn instrument to summon neighbours

Despite the bleak setting and the weight of the topics covered, Pyre is suffused with humour. The central couple are delightful. Like many long-married spouses, they seem to treat bickering as a love language.

Kapri, who is from Uttarakhand, got the idea for the film in 2018 after meeting an 84-year-old man in Munsiyari, a scenic hill town in the state.

"I visited him after seeing his photo in a Facebook post. The wrinkles on his face really fascinated me. His face was unique."

Kapri said he asked him and his wife what their biggest worry was.

"He said, 'My biggest worry is, if I die first, who is going to take care of her?' And she said, 'He doesn't know how to cook. So if I die first, I don't know who is going to cook food for him.' That was so heartwarming for me."

Kapri says he initially tried to make his film with "the real couple", but abandoned the idea after a week of shooting, when it became clear it was not working. He then approached actors Naseeruddin Shah and Ratna Pathak - a couple themselves - for the lead roles.

Shah loved the script, Kapri says, but felt that he and Pathak did not belong to the region and would struggle to do justice to the characters.

Kapri finally found his Padam Singh within his own family – his father's younger brother, a retired army soldier who expressed an interest in acting. He found his Tulsi in another village. Heera Devi, an elderly widow, had raised her children through years of farming, cutting grass and tending to her buffalo.

Their tender love story has won hearts in India

Over the years, Padam Singh and Heera Devi tell the BBC, they have watched stories of ghost villages, of children migrating for work, abandoning the elderly, play out all around them. They say today they are overwhelmed by the attention Pyre has got.

Since 2024, the film has been screened at some of the world's biggest festivals. It has won 18 awards, Kapri says, including three for best feature and 12 audience-choice best film prizes.

Despite its success at festivals, Kapri says, Pyre spent two years without a distributor. Even OTT platforms passed on the film and it finally reached cinemas only when a producer friend of his stepped in to fund a theatrical release.

But, he says, the modest 70-screen release on 30 October sparked favourable word-of-mouth reviews and with the demand for tickets going up, there was an increase in overall screenings too.

Meanwhile, the misgivings that both Padam Singh and Heera Devi say they initially had about stepping in front of the camera and forgetting their lines are gone now.

Heera Devi says she was even concerned about what her children would think - and what would society say?

Today she and Padam Singh are basking in the positive reviews of film critics and the affection of their audiences.

Padam Singh and Heera Devi's story is also one of ghost villages, children migrating for work and abandoned elderly

Heera Devi says the film has appealed to many because "in reality, our village is just like this".

They have met teary-eyed people at multiple screenings - many wanting to touch their feet and hug them, many who said the film reminded them of their own parents and grandparents who are waiting in villages, towns and cities that they had come from.

"We felt immense joy and happiness. We've received so much love and inspiration - something we had never imagined," says Padam Singh.

But the best moment for him came when he met Naseeruddin Shah in Mumbai. "He watched the entire movie and had tears in his eyes. He hugged me. He said, 'Bubu, the role you have performed, I wouldn't be able to pull off even in seven lifetimes.'"

The film's appeal, Heera Devi says, is because "in reality, our village is just like this".

"Across villages in India, the elderly are left alone. No one's children stay at home anymore and it's the same situation for all parents. They keep waiting for their son and daughter-in-law, hoping that their grandchildren would visit and spend a few days with them. The loneliness is simply unbearable."

Padam Singh says he has a message for the younger generation in Uttarakhand and the rest of India.

"I want to tell them they must not abandon their motherland, the land where they were born," he says. "I also appeal to the government to bring education and employment to where people are - so that they don't have to wander away. When that happens, the parents who are being left behind will also be cared for."

Tesla will wind down production of its Cybertruck vehicles at its Texas factory next year, Elon Musk says.

He did not spell out whether it plans to stop making them entirely or shift production elsewhere, but did say the decision was to "make room" for building more of its self-driving Cybercab cars.

But the project's lead engineer, Wes Morrill, appeared to suggest the vehicle was being discontinued, writing on X: "Cybertruck was an incredible technology development platform and lives on through Cybercab."

With its distinctive angular looks, the Cybertruck attracted diehard fans, but was beset by delays before being launched in 2023 and has had disappointing sales numbers since.

Tesla fans have been mourning the news online, with one person calling it " the best vehicle Tesla has ever made , external " as he lamented it being "discontinued next year".

Musk responded to the user , external with the word "true", adding: "But the Cybertruck fleet will be around for a long time."

Tesla's stock rose 4.7% on Friday after his announcement.

The vehicle has always been a passion project for Musk. He said it was " way more awesome than people realise , external " in March, and called it the " best product Tesla has ever made to date , external " in April.

But there have always been big questions about whether consumers shared that view and whether the Cybertruck could cut through and earn a spot in the US' lucrative truck market.

It was not helped by inauspicious introduction to the public in 2019 when Musk attempted to show off the Cybertruck's apparently unbreakable glass, only for it to shatter during a live demonstration.

Despite the gaffe, the Cybertruck ended up receiving a 146,000 orders, Musk said in 2019 , while it was still in development.

In the end, the vehicle launched in 2023, keeping its novel design - an angular shape with a body made of stainless steel.

In 2025, Tesla sold just 20,237 Cybertrucks, a decline from 38,965 a year earlier, according to figures from Kelley Blue Book.

Musk had predicted annual sales of 250,000 after commercial production of Cybertruck began in 2023.

Tesla fans praised its retro-futuristic look, which some said looked like something " straight out of Blade Runner , external ".

But critics were far less kind, joking about its appearance and labelling it " ugly as sin , external ".

Several recalls - including in 2025 affecting more than 46,000 Cybertrucks over concerns part of its trim could fall off - would not have helped.

"We need to make it at a price that people can afford," Musk told Wall Street analysts that year - which ended up being $61,000 (then £48,000) for all the "bells and whistles".

In 2026, the so-called "Cyberbeast" model comes in at $102,000.

Shares in artificial intelligence and technology firms have recovered slightly from an enormous sell-off that wiped trillions of dollars off stock values.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq stock index closed in positive territory following a market rout that began in the US on Thursday before spilling over to Asian and European markets into Friday.

Investors had been selling off tech shares in part due to concerns the Democrat victory in the midterm elections would mean slower artificial intelligence development.

However the latest US employment figures added to a mixed picture for American markets on Friday morning, with an unexpectedly strong 165,000 jobs added to the economy in September.

On Thursday, businesses closely linked to artificial intelligence development took a hammering on stock markets, particularly chip and semiconductor makers.

But the Nasdaq Composite bounced back slightly on Friday, ending the day up 1.1%, partly reversing some of its 5.5% fall.

The S&P 500, which tracks the share prices of the largest publicly-traded US companies, closed up 0.3%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average was flat through the day before ending slightly down 0.4%.

Companies that lost hundreds of billions in market value recovered some ground on Friday, including Nvidia, SpaceX and Tesla.

However, stock markets in Asia and Europe fared worse.

The Kospi in South Korea closed down 6% on Friday, with shares in chipmaker SK Hynix plunging more than 10%. European markets also fell, with the main indexes in Germany, France and Spain ending the day down.

In the UK, the FTSE 100, which tracks the largest companies on the London Stock Exchange, declined 1.01%.

In addition to the recent market volatility, UK traders were also digesting the latest Bank of England decision to raise interest rates and the signal that another rate rise could be on the cards to curb rising prices.

The market fluctuations also come after the sweeping Democrat victory in the midterm elections.

A number of Democrats campaigned for new rules and regulations for artificial intelligence (AI) and data centres, and the party has since won control of both houses of congress as well as key contests in states that have been part of the AI data centre race.

US President Donald Trump on Friday reiterated his supported for what he calls "super intelligence", saying only "foolish leadership" would "say no to the riches they bring".

However, there have also been concerns over whether the enormous amounts of money being spent on AI will pay off.

Russ Shaw, founder of global tech advocacy firm Tech London Advocates, said the election result was sending a message that a rethink was needed on AI.

"The incoming Congress is going to really focus on AI in a very dramatic way," he told the BBC's Business Today.

"I'm a big fan of AI, but I'm watching what these companies are doing, and they're not communicating effectively at all, particularly in the US, about what the benefits of AI are all about."

Pierre Baqué, chief executive of AI platform Neural Concept, said the share movements were a "necessary market correction" that reflected a legitimate concern about the amount of money being poured into AI infrastructure.

"The industry must move beyond unchecked infrastructure investment and demonstrate greater financial discipline," he said.

"We are entering a critical transition phase, a market purgatory where raw tech must prove its widespread economic value."

Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, said it had been a brutal week for markets, and the key question was whether the jump in the S&P 500 and Nasdaq would be sustained.

"Once investors have had the weekend to catch their breath, next week could give a clearer indication of whether the tech trade is going down the pan or fighting back."

Could the US midterms put a pin in the AI bubble?

Elon Musk appears to signal the end of the road for Cybertruck

As well as the fallout of the midterms and the plunge in artificial intelligence stocks, US traders will also be digesting the latest jobs figures.

And those numbers were better than expected: US employers added 165,000 new jobs in October, well above the average monthly increase and more than double what analysts had expected.

Overall the unemployment rate, which counts the number of people who are out of work but actively looking for a job, eased slightly to 4.1% from 4.2% in September .

The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) said the unemployment rate has remained in the narrow range of 4.1% to 4.3% since March.

Neil Birrell, chief investment officer at investment firm Premier Miton, said while the jobs figures may feel like second billing to the market movements they were still important.

"The US economy is running hard which may mean the risks the markets are worrying about at the moment are not such a risk to the real economy as is being feared," he said.

MN202611_1wray9ln09j.t: Rwanda insists on pushing for changes in international law to provide for reparations to survivors of the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi, citing the gaps of the legal framework governing the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda (ICTR) which did not provide for compensation for the suffering they endured. ALSO READ: Expert explains Africa's efforts to seek colonial reparations Minister of Justice Emmanuel Ugirashebuja said although the tribunal prosecuted and convicted genocide perpetrators, its mandate did not include provisions for reparations to victims, leaving their losses and suffering unaddressed through that process. He was speaking in Kigali on Friday, November 6, during the 15th Annual Conference of the African Society of International Law (AfSIL), which is examining Africa's experience with reparations under international law. ALSO READ: Will there ever be reparations for Genocide survivors? Ugirashebuja said the conference provides an opportunity to examine whether existing international legal instruments can address such gaps, and what reforms may be necessary to ensure victims of serious crimes can obtain redress. “When the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda (ICTR) was established to prosecute genocide-related crimes, the laws governing it did not provide for reparations for the suffering caused. This is a clear gap: a genocide occurred, and people were directly affected by it, yet no provision was made for reparations,” he said. He noted that survivors lost family members, sustained physical injuries and had their property destroyed, while many continue to experience emotional suffering. ALSO READ: Global migration experts to assess reparations for Genocide survivors Although reparations cannot restore lives or undo the consequences of the Genocide, the minister said they remain an important way of addressing the harm suffered by victims. “Although compensation for emotional suffering cannot erase what happened, it represents an attempt to rectify past wrongs,” he said. He added that the question goes beyond Rwanda, given Africa's history of slavery, colonialism, genocide and other serious crimes, whose consequences continue to affect communities. ALSO READ: SURVIVORS’ REPARATIONS, A DELICATE ISSUE The discussions, he said, should help establish who qualifies for reparations, who bears responsibility and what form the remedies should take, including compensation for moral damages. ALSO READ: What happens to Félicien Kabuga’s assets after his death? Calls for review of traditional legal framework Judge Dire Tladi of the International Court of Justice (ICJ) said the challenge extends beyond the ICTR, arguing that the international legal framework governing reparations has not kept pace with developments in international law, particularly the recognition of human rights, genocide and crimes against humanity. He said traditional principles of state responsibility and reparation largely reflect legal thinking from the 1920s, when the framework was developed, and were not designed to address the scale of harm caused by mass atrocities or environmental destruction. “Some of the challenges, I mean the main challenge is that the law on reparation is an old law, and it hasn't really changed with time. It hasn't moved with time,” he said. Tladi argued that the traditional approach also faces difficulties when dealing with widespread harm involving multiple victims, where the consequences cannot easily be quantified or reversed. He cited the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi and other mass atrocities as examples of situations where compensation cannot restore what victims and entire communities have lost. “The types of injuries suffered in these types of regions are not easily quantifiable, and the notion that any form of reparation can wipe out the consequences is simply untenable and unsustainable,” he said. He also pointed to climate change as another area exposing the limitations of existing rules, particularly where several countries contribute to environmental damage while vulnerable nations bear much of its impact. Referring to the ICJ's 2025 advisory opinion on climate change, Tladi said the court outlined the general legal framework for determining state responsibility but left questions about how responsibility and reparations should be established in specific cases. He said such challenges require further examination by international law scholars and practitioners, rather than expecting courts to develop new legal principles without sufficient consideration. Tladi urged African countries to work together in shaping the future of international law, arguing that their collective position would be important in influencing how reparations are addressed globally. ALSO READ: Rwanda to host major conference on colonial reparations Africa urged to develop common reparations agenda Moïse Makane Mbengue, president of the African Society of International Law, said African countries need to develop a common position on reparations that reflects the continent's priorities, rather than limiting their demands to financial compensation. He cited the return of cultural property taken from African countries during colonialism as one form of reparation, arguing that restitution may be more appropriate than monetary compensation. On climate change, he said African countries should also consider measures such as debt relief and cancellation, alongside mechanisms that provide resources to help them adapt to its effects. “Reparations are not just about compensation. Quite often in the African conversation, when we talk about reparation for historical injustices, we think in terms of compensation. But there are other mechanisms that should be thought about beyond compensation,” he said. Mbengue said international law provides room to identify and develop different remedies, but African countries must take a more active role in shaping the rules. He recommended what he observes as “Africanisation of international law”, saying the continent should move beyond simply following legal approaches and interpretations developed elsewhere. He also called for unity among African states, arguing that a common position would strengthen their influence in international discussions and negotiations. Using climate change as an example, Mbengue said Africa has contributed a relatively small share of global greenhouse gas emissions but faces significant consequences from the crisis. He said African countries therefore need a shared strategy on loss and damage, including agreement on the mechanisms through which they should benefit from reparations. The conference, running from November 6 to 7, brings together international law scholars, judges, practitioners and policymakers to examine how African experiences of historical and contemporary injustices can inform the development of international law.

Hashize iminsi humvikana umwuka utari mwiza hagati ya Muyoboke Alex, usanzwe afasha The Ben mu bikorwa bya muzika, na Nduwimana Jean Paul uzwi nka Noopja Noopja, inshuti magara y’uyu muhanzi. Amakuru avuga ko kimwe mu byatumye umubano w’aba bombi urushaho kuzamo agatotsi ari urugendo The Ben yagiriye muri Uganda.

The Ben yari yatumiwe mu gitaramo cyo kwizihiza imyaka 10 ishize Comedy Store itangiye, igikorwa gitegurwa n’umunyarwenya w’Umunya-Uganda, Alex Muhangi ku wa 30 Ukwakira 2026.

Mbere y’urwo rugendo, byari biteganyijwe ko The Ben azaherekezwa n’abantu barindwi, ariko umubare w’abagombaga kujyana na we uza kugabanywa ugera kuri bane gusa, bisabwe n’uwateguye icyo gitaramo.

Bivugwa ko Alex Muhangi yamenyesheje The Ben n’abantu bamufashaga mu rugendo n'igitaramo yari afite muri Uganda di bari mu ikipe ko mu matike arindwi bari bamusabye yabashije kubona ane gusa.

Aha rero byahise bisaba ko habaho guhitamo abantu bagombaga. Ariko kandi hari amakuru y'uko nubwo Noopja yagaragaje ko uwatumye ibyangombwa bye bisigara ari Alex Muyoboke hari amakuru ahamya ko Muyoboke mu byo yari yaroherereje Muhangi harimo na Passport ya Noopja.

Muri iryo hinduka, Noopja yasigaye mu bantu batagombaga kujyana na The Ben muri Uganda, ibintu bivugwa ko byarushijeho kuzamura umwuka mubi hagati ye na Muyoboke Alex. Ndetse bikavugwa ko The Ben ubwe ariwe wahisemo abagombaga kujyana nawe.

Ni mugihe abandi bavuga ko Muyoboke Alex, wari ufite uruhare mu gutegura gahunda z’urugendo rwa The Ben, ari we waba waragize uruhare mu gutuma Noopja atajyana n’uyu muhanzi bikazamura umwuka mubi hagati y'aba bombi.

Mu gushaka igisubizo cy'uburyo Noopja atasigara, The Ben yaje gufata icyemezo cyo kumwishyurira urugendo n’aho yagombaga gucimbika muri hoteli, kugira ngo adasigara nyamara yarari ku rutonde rw'abagombaga kumuhereza muri Uganda.

Noopja ubwo yageraga muri Uganda, bivugwa ko atari yishimiye Alex Muyoboke, kubera uburyo yamufashe mu myiteguro y’urugendo kuko ngo byageze aho Noopja yandikira Muyoboke ubutumwa, amugaragariza ko yamuhemukiye kandi ko na we azamwishyura.

Noopja na Muyoboke Alex ni abantu bamaze igihe mu ruganda rw’imyidagaduro mu Rwanda, aho bagiye bagira uruhare mu bikorwa bitandukanye by’abahanzi. Icyakora, ibyabaye mu rugendo rwa Uganda byongeye kugaragaza ko hari ibibazo bitarakemuka hagati yabo.

Kugeza ubu, biracyari ikibazo cyakuruye impaka ku mubano w’aba bombi n'uruhare rwabo mu bikorwa bya The Ben nubwo aya makimbirane hagati y'aba bombi atari aya vuba nk'uko aba hafi y'aba bombi babivuga.

Charlene Ruto, umukobwa wa Perezida wa Kenya, William Ruto, yasezeranye na Isaya Yunge mu birori byitabiriwe n’abashyitsi batandukanye barimo abayobozi n’abandi bantu bakomeye.

Perezida wa Kenya, William Ruto, yagaragaje ibyishimo n’ishema yatewe no kubona umukobwa we, Charlene Ruto, ashinga urugo na Isaya Yunge, mu bukwe bwabereye i Mwanza muri Tanzania.

Mu butumwa yandikiye umukobwa we, Ruto yavuze ko nta kindi gishimisha umubyeyi nko kubona umukobwa we abona urukundo, ibyishimo n’umuntu bazafatanya kubaka ejo hazaza.

Yavuze ko yishimira urugendo Charlene yagize kuva akiri umwana muto ubwo yamukuriraga mu maboko, kugeza ubwo abaye umugore uhamye, urangwa n’impuhwe n’izindi ndangagaciro.

Perezida Ruto yagize ati: “Mu gihe wowe na Yunge mwahanaga indahiro zo gushyingiranwa muri Mwanza muri Tanzania, umutima wanjye wari wuzuye ishema, gushimira Imana n’ibyishimo bikomeye.”

Yongeye kugaragaza ko kubona umukobwa we atangira urugendo rushya rw’ubuzima ari kimwe mu bihe by’agaciro gakomeye kuri we nk’umubyeyi.

Mbere y’ubukwe bwabereye muri Tanzania uyu munsi, Charlene Ruto yanateguye igikorwa cy’amasengesho yo kumusabira umugisha mbere yo gutangira ubuzima bw’urushako, kizwi nka ‘Mother’s Blessing’. Iki gikorwa cyitabiriwe na nyina, Madamu Rachel Ruto, hamwe n’abandi bagore bakuru bo mu muryango, basengera Charlene bamusabira umugisha n’urugendo rwiza mu buzima bushya agiye gutangira.

Nyuma y’ayo masengesho, hakurikiyeho ibirori byo gusezera ku buzima bw’ubukumi (Bridal Shower) byabereye i Nairobi, mbere y’uko ubukwe nyirizina bubera i Mwanza muri Tanzania.

Gusa, icyo gihe ngo byari byiza kuko hari abakozi bo mu ngo baza bakamara igihe, umwe akaba yamara nk’imyaka itanu cyangwa irenga, akabona gutaha, agashaka undi nawe akaba yamara indi myaka bityo bityo.

Ubu amaze imyaka 8 adakoresha abakozi bakora baba mu rugo, kubera ko yari asigaye ashaka umukozi, akamara ukwezi kumwe akagenda, undi yaza akamara iminsi itatu, cyangwa se akaba Yamara n’umunsi umwe bugacya avuga ko atahakunze, akagenda.

Yagize ati,” Ubu hashize imyaka 8, nararetse burundu gukoresha abakozi baba mu ngo, kubera ko byari bimaze kuntesha umutwe. Njya kubareka burundu, umwana wanjye muto yari afite imyaka 9. Nari naramenyereye gukoresha abakobwa baza tukamara imyaka itanu cyangwa irenga, uwa nyuma muri abo twatindanye agiye, natangiye kugira ibibazo hakaza bahita bagenda, umwe yaraje amara ukwezi ati nagize ibyago ndatashye sinzagaruka, undi aje amara iminsi itatu ati sinkunda kurara mu nzu yo hanze ndatashye, undi aje amara umunsi umwe bucya ataha, kuva ubwo niyemeza kutazongera kubashaka”.

Ubu Musengamana, ngo akoresha abakozi baza bagakora imirimo runaka hanyuma bagataha. Abo bakora bataha, ngo ntibagorana cyane nk’ababa mu ngo iminsi yose, kubera ko baraza niba ari ukumesa imyenda bakamesa, ibyo byarangira bakitahira. Niba ari ugukora isuku mu busitani baraza bagakora ibyo bagataha.Mbese abo bakora bataha ngo bamworohereza ubuzima kuko baraza bagakora icyo yabahamagariye gusa bakitahira.

Yagize ati,” Muri iyo myaka ishize ndetse gukoresha abakozi bo mu rugo bahoraho, nabonye harimo ibyiza byinshi nubwo nzi ko bigoye ku bantu bagifite abana bato.Buriya abenshi muri bo, bagira ukuntu bangiza cyane, ariko ubu kubera ko ari njyewe ubyikorera, njya guhaha bijyanye n’abantu mfite mu rugo, iyo nteka, nteka bijyanye n’umubare w’abantu bahari ngateka ibishira, kandi abakozi wasanga batetse byinshi, hagasigara ibyo bamena mu mifuka.Gaz ndayitekesha nkarambirwa, ariko icyo gihe nkibakoresha ntiyamaraga Kabiri.Kwikorera akazi ko mu rugo birananiza ku mubiri kuko bisaba imbaraga n’umwanya, ariko mu mutwe uba wumva umeze neza, nta muntu wirirwa atuma uvuga nabi, umubwiriza, n’ibindi. Ubu abana barakuze bose, bari no mu kazi ariko bambwiye ko rwose tuzakomeza kwikorera akazi kuko nta mukozi bashaka uza kuba mu rugo…”.

Umukozi uza gufasha mu byo kumesa cyangwa no gutunganya mu busitani kwa Musengamana, ngo aza inshuro eshatu mu kwezi, hanyuma akamuhemba 40.000 by’Amafaranga y’u Rwanda, kandi yumva ari igiciro cyiza, kubera ko abyumvikanaho nawe, bijyanye n’akazi aba yakoze.

Mukamwezi Chantal, atuye muri Kimironko, afite abana babiri bakiri bato, we bimusaba kuba afite abakozi bo mu rugo babiri bakora baba mu rugo, kuko we afite akazi akora gatuma agenda mu gitonda akagaruka ku mugoroba. Abana bafite umwe afite imyaka 3, umuto afite umwaka 1.

Umukozi umwe w’umuhungu ashinzwe guteka, n’indi mirimo yo mu rugo harimo no koza imodoka mu gitondo, mu gihe uw’umukobwa ashinzwe kwita ku bana,harimo kubagaburira, kubamesera n’ibindi.

Yagize ati,” Abakozi bo mu ngo muri iki gihe babaye imari pe, njyewe nkoresha babiri kuko mfite abana bato kandi sinirirwa mu rugo. Ukora imirimo yo mu gikoni w’umuhungu muhemba 50.000Frw ku kwezi, naho umukobwa urera abana, nkamuhemba 35. 000 ku kwezi. Muri rusange,nsohora 85.000Frw ku kwezi agenewe abakozi. Kandi buriya no kubatunga ubwabyo birahenda, kuko ibyo bakoresha byose mu rugo, ni njyewe ubigura.Njyewe ntibyanyorohera kubaho nta mukozi, kubera ko ubwo akazi kanjye kahita gahagarara.Gusa bisigaye bigoye, yaba amafaranga bahembwa yabaye menshi, ariko noneho no kuboneka ntibakiboneka nk’uko byari bimeze mbere”.

Kamanzi Jacky, atuye mu Karere ka Kicukiro, afite umugabo n’abana batatu, umwana muto afite imyaka 6, yaba we n’umugabo we, ntabwo birirwa mu rugo, bazinduka bajya ku kazi, kandi n’abana babo bose ngo biga ku mashuri birirwayo bagataha saa kumi z’umugoroba. Nyuma yo kubona ko nta muntu uba uri mu rugo, ngo bahisemo gukoresha umukozi wo mu rugo uza buri munsi, ariko agataha nimugoroba amaze gutegura amafunguro y’ijoro.

Yagize ati, “ Twararebye dusanga nta mpamvu, yo gushaka uriya mukozi uba mu rugo ku buryo buhoraho, kubera ko nta muntu wirirwa mu rugo, yaba njyewe simpiriwa, yaba abana na papa wabo twese tuzinduka tugenda, ubwo mu gitondo nzinduka ntegura abana, tukabasiga ku ishuri tugakomeza ku kazi. Uwo nashatse ukora ariko agataha, aza saa moya za mu gitondo agataha saa kumi n’ebyiri z’umugoroba, ataha hafi y’aho dutuye, ntabwo ari kure. Muhemba 60.000 Frw ku kwezi, ariko hari nubwo njya nyuzamo nkamuha icyo nakwita nk’agahimbazamusyi, bitewe n’uko mbona akazi kagenze neza, njya nyuzamo nkabikora, nubwo ntavuga ngo ni ku buryo buhoraho”. Kamanzi avuga ko iyo urebye ayo mafaranga yishyura uwo mukozi umufasha nubwo akora ataha,ubona ari menshi, ariko nanone wareba uko ibiciro bisigaye bimeze ku masoko, ukabona ko atari menshi cyane. Nk’uwo umukorera, ngo ni umubyeyi ufite umwana agomba kwitaho, bivuze ko aba agomba guhaha muri ayo mafaranga no kwita ku mwana we, n’ibindi bikenerwa mu buzima bwa buri munsi.

Yagize ati, “ Ubuzima bwarahenze, ku buryo n’ayo mafaranga duha aba bantu badufasha mu kazi ko mu rugo ubara ukabona ni macye, ahubwo bibaye bikunda twayongera, ahubwo ikibazo ni uko natwe ubushobozi buba butari bwinshi. Nonese ibi dukenera mu ngo nabo babikenera byose, urumva biba byoroshye! Gusa baradufasha cyane, turabakeneye, nubwo amafaranga yo kubahemba yakomeza kwiyongera tuzakomeza kubashaka. Buriya mu rugo haba akazi kenshi biragoye ko twakikorera ngo tuzabone n’uko tujya gushaka amafaranga. Ahubwo ubu ikibazo gihari kinakomeye, ni uko batakiboneka cyane. Cyera wasangaga udashobora gushaka umukozi wo mu rugo ngo umare iminsi ibiri utaramubona, ariko ubu wamara n’icyumweru, ushakisha hose, yaza bugacya agenda, mbese bisigaye bigoye…”.

Ahitwa mu Mariba ya Bukunzi ni ho hari ivubiro rya Ndagano wategekaga u Bukunzi ku mwaduko w’abazungu. Bukunzi yari iherereye mu Majyepfo y’Uburengerazuba bw’u Rwanda, ihana imbibi n’uturere tw’u Busozo, i Cyesha, Impara, na Biru ndetse n’igihugu cy’u Burundi.

U Rwanda rwigarurira i Kinyaga mu kinyejana cya 18, u Bukunzi bwari mu gice cyafashwe n’umutwe w’ingabo z’Impara, ari na cyo cyatumye aho hantu hose hitwa Impara.

Mu mpera z’icyo kinyejana, Umwami Kigeri III Ndabarasa yategetse umutware w’Impara, Rwanteri, kugabira u Bukunzi umuvubyi witwaga Kija. Kuva ubwo u Bukunzi bwabaye impugu yigenga itegekwa n’Abami b’Abavubyi bakomoka kuri Kija, bagatura ikoro umwami w’u Rwanda ndetse n’umutware w’Impara.

Abanditsi b’amateka bavuga ko Kija yageze mu Bukunzi akomotse i Rwingi hakurya ya Rusizi. Kubera ubuhanga yari afite bwo kuvuba imvura, uwo muvubyi ntiyatinze kumenyekana no kuba ikirangirire mu Rwanda. Umwami amumenye amugabira u Bukunzi kugira ngo ajye amuvubira imvura igihe yabuze.

Uko imigenderanire hagati y’Abami b’u Rwanda n’ab’u Bukunzi yarushagaho kuba myiza, abami b’u Rwanda babagabiraga indi misozi, u Bukunzi buraguka buba impugu nini igizwe n’imisozi ya Nyamubembe, Mutare, Nkungu, Nyakabuye, Karambo, Mwezi, Karengera, Kanyinya, Gitambi, Cyingwa, Rubona, Kaboza, Mahonga, Cyimpundu, Kigurwe, Mwiyando, Mubori, Rwintare, Rurama, Wanyangura, Rwinkuba, Kibazi, Gaseke, Matyazo na Rwabidege.

Abatware ndetse n’umwami w’u Rwanda baturaga Abami bo mu Bukunzi kugira ngo babagushirize imvura mu Gihugu. Buri gihe uko umwami asabye imvura ikagwa, yahaga umuvubyi inka nibura eshanu ndetse n’impfizi yazo.

Uretse kuvuba imvura, abami bo mu Bukunzi ngo bari bafite ububasha budasanzwe bwo kwirukana inzige n’utundi dukoko twangiza imyaka, bakarumbura imirima, bakavura inka ndetse bagatuma zigira imitavu myiza.

Kuva u Bukunzi bubaye impugu yigenga kugeza igihe yavaniweho n’abakoroni b’Ababirigi mu w’1925, yategetswe n’Abami barindwi kandi bose bari Abavubyi. Abo ni Kija I Gisuma, Ngoga, Kabeja, Ruzigamanzi, Kija II, Ndagano Ruhagata na Ngoga Bihigimondo.

Buri gihe uko umwami w’u Rwanda yatangaga hakima undi, impugu y’u Bukunzi yatangaga abantu babiri bagapfa, bakaba ‘imisego y’umwami’. Hatangwaga umuhungu n’umukobwa, umuhungu akajugunywa mu gishanga cya Nyagafunzo kiri hafi yo ku Karambo, naho umurambo w’umukobwa bakawohereza i Bumbogo.

Umwami Ruganzu II Ndori ngo ni we wategetse abanyabukunzi kujya batanga imisego y’umwami. Umunsi umwe Ruganzu arambagira Igihugu, yageze mu Bugarama imwe mu mpfizi ze iva mu zindi irarorongotana igera ku mugezi w’amashyuza. Abacuku ni ukuvuga abo mu muryango w’Abacuku bayibonye barayifata. Ruganzu yakurikiye ikirari cyayo, ageze aho asanga barangije kuyibaga.

Abasaba ku nyama zayo, izo bamuhaye azitunga ku icumu rye, azamuka iya Bukunzi. Ageze i Nyamubembe, ahura n’umugabo wo mu bwoko bw’Abayombo, aramuhagarika amwaka za nyama.

Ruganzu abonye ibimubayeho ariyamira ati: « Mwa banyabukunzi mwe, mugize kumbagira impfizi, none munyaze n’inyama zayo”! Ruganzu arumirwa, ngo ni ko kuvuga ati: « Uko umwami yimye i Rwanda, mujye mutanga igitambo cy’umukobwa w’Umucuku n’umuhungu w’Umuyombo”. Ngiyo inkomoko y’imisego y’umwami yaturukaga mu Bukunzi!

Mu myaka ya nyuma y’ingoma y’ u Bukunzi, uwamenyekanye cyane ni umugabekazi Nyirandakunze. Uyu mugabekazi yari umugore wa Ndagano, akaba nyina wa Ngoga Bihigimondo, umwami wa nyuma wa Bukunzi. Nyirandakunze yavukaga mu Busozo, akaba igishegabo, ndetse ngo ni we wategekeraga umuhungu we.

Nk’uko bivugwa n’abatuye ahahoze ari mu Bukunzi ndetse barimo n’Umushambo witwa Bazakiruru Innocent ukomoka kuri Ndagano, ngo Ndagano yubatse inzu nziza cyane y’umuratwa, ifite igisenge kiboshye nk’ikibo, ashaka kuyirongoreramo undi mugore kuko yabonaga Nyirandakunze ari igishegabo gikabije.

Umwamikazi agira ishyari aritewe n’uko agiye guharikwa, ndetse ababazwa n’iyo nzu atazaturamo. Ikindi kandi na we yashakaga ko umuhungu we ari we uzasimbura se ku ngoma y’u Bukunzi. Ibyo byose ngo byatumye acisha amarozi, yica Ndagano akiri muto. Bavuga ko yamutunze inkaka y’ingona ikamukenya.

Nyuma y’urupfu rwa Ndagano rwabaye ku wa 30 Werurwe 1923 Nyirandakunze yimukiye muri ya nzu y’umuratwa, yimana ingoma n’umuhungu we Ngoga Bihigimondo. Kuko Ngoga yari akiri muto, yategekerwaga na nyina hamwe na se wabo witwaga Bigirumwera. Ubutegetsi bw’abakoroni b’Ababirigi bwafataga ubwami bwa Bukunzi nk’ubwigometse kuko bwanze kubayoboka ngo butange imisoro n’abantu bo gukora imirimo ya Teritwari. Ibyo byatumye Adiminisitarateri wa Teritwari ya Cyangugu witwaga Bwana Keyser ategura igitero cyo guhirika ingoma y’u Bukunzi.

Bigirumwera amenye ko u Bukunzi bugiye guterwa yasabye Padiri mukuru wa Mibirizi witwaga P.Knoll kumuhuza n’Ababirigi, arabikora ariko biranga biba iby’ubusa.

Ubutegetsi bw’Ababirigi bufatanyije na Rwagataraka wategekaga i Kinyaga bwagabye ibitero bitatu mu Bukunzi. Icya mbere cyagabwe muri Mata 1923, kigabwa n’abasirikare boherejwe na Keyser; kiratsindwa. Icya kabiri cyagabwe n’ingabo zoherejwe na Adiminisitarateri Fiolle tariki 12-14 Werurwe 1924, i Bwami barahunga.

Icyo gihe ngo Nyirandakunze yahungiye mu ishyamba cyimeza rya Cyamudongo aribamo umwaka wose. Iryo shyamba Nyirandakunze yahungiyemo ubu ni igice cya Pariki y’Igihugu ya Nyungwe, ariko abaturage barituriye baryita Ishyamba rya Nyirandakunze cyangwa mu Ryanyirandakunze.

Igitero cya nyuma ari na cyo cyatsinze u Bukunzi cyagabwe tariki 09 Werurwe 1925. Aho umwami n’umugabekazi bihishe hari hamenyekanye bahatera mu ijoro ryo kuri iyo tariki, Nyirandakunze baramurasa kuko yarwanyije abaje kumufata, Ngoga arakomereka arafatwa ajya gufungirwa i Kigali ari na ho yaguye mu Ukwakira 1925, naho Bigirumwera aracika ahungira muri Repubulika Iharanira Demokarasi ya Kongo. Ingoma y’u Bukunzi ihera ityo.

Aho amavubiro ya Ndagano yahoze hitwa mu Bwiza bwa Bweramvura ya Mataba. Ubu ni ku nkengero z’ishyamba rya Cyamudongo, mu Mudugudu wa Rwamaraba, Akagari ka Mataba, mu Murenge wa Nkungu, Akarere ka Rusizi; ku muhanda uva i Nkungu ujya mu Mataba. Ni agashanga gato karimo amazi menshi, gafite ubuso nk’ubwa metero kare 150, karimo ibyatsi by’imigugu babohesha ibirago, igiti cy’umugano, igihondohondo n’imizibira. Ako gashanga gakikijwe n’imirima bahingamo ibigori, ibisheke, n’ibindi.

Mu Bwiza bwa Bweramvura ya Mataba, ahahoze amavubiro ya Bukunzi

Muri ako gashanga ngo kera harimo amahembe Ndagano yavubishaga. Abahatuye bavuga ko yari amahembe abiri y’inzovu iry’ingore n’iry’ingabo. Ku ngoma ya Kayibanda, umutwa witwaga Rwibasira ngo yakuyemo ihembe rimwe arishyira bene Ndagano aho bari barahungiye i Murenge. Irindi hembe ngo riracyarimo kugeza magingo aya, akaba ari yo mpamvu abahahinga n’abahaturiye birinda kunywa amazi yaho, dore ko ngo n’iyo bahahinga babona igishanga gitigita!

Mu Bwiza bwa Bweramvura ya Mataba hahanamiwe n’agasozi ka Rwamaraba, ngo akaba ariko Ndagano yicaragaho avuye kuvuba ari kumwe n’umutwa witwaga Rudakemwa wamutwazaga ingoma na yo yakoreshwaga muri iyo mihango.

Ni bimwe mu byo bagarutseho mu cyumweru gishize, ubwo iyo Komisiyo yagezaga ku Nteko Ishinga Amategeko, imitwe yombi, raporo y’ibikorwa byayo by’umwaka ushize wa 2025-2026, inagaragaza ibyo iteganya uyu mwaka.

Nyuma yo gusobanura no kugaragariza Inteko Ishinga Amategeko uko umwaka ushize wagenze no kugaragaza ibyo bateganya muri uyu, Depite Christine Bakundufite yabajije ikibazo cyagaragajwe na Perezida wa Komisiyo Providence Umurungi, cy’umusore basanze agarutse mu igororero ry'ibanze inshuro icyenda, abaza niba barasuzumye impamvu ibimutera niba nta kindi kibazo cyihariye basanze afite.

Mu gusubiza iki kibazo Umurungi yavuze ko ari mu itsinda ryagiye gusura Igororero ry’ibanze rya Gikondo (ahazwi nko kwa Kabuga).

Ati “Iyo umurebye ni umusore mwiza cyane, umurebye utanavuga ko afite ikibazo cyo mu mutwe, ariko afatirwa ubujura Musanze, bamurekura ejo agafatirwa Rubavu. Wagira ngo ni ibintu yiyemeje, sinkeka ko uko yari ameze n’uko asa, sinavuga ko ari umuntu wari ufite ikibazo uvuga ngo mu muryango wenda nintaha ndabura icyo ndya. Hari abo usanga nk’abo ngabo ari ingeso nyine yamwokamye, yumva ko agomba guhora muri ibyo bibazo gusa.”

Si mu magororero y’ibanze gusa uwo musore amaze kujyanwa kuko basanze yaranajyanwe mu bigo ngororamuco inshuro zirenze imwe nkuko Umurungi abisobanura.

Ati “Uwo nguwo twasanze yarajyanywe Iwawa nka 3, mu igororero ry’ibanze yari ahaje nka 6, ariko Iwawa yagiyeyo 3. Hari uwo ureba ugasanga wakora ubuvugizi, wagira ute, baramurekura ejo bakaba bagonganye na we. Nk’uwo yari ikibazo cyihariye, ariko ubundi abandi bagaruka inshuro zirenze imwe, ni cyane cyane ibijyanye n’ubujura cyangwa se ibiyobyabwenge. Ibiyobyabwenge akaba yaragiye nk’Iwawa akabibura, akamarayo wa mwaka bamarayo biga, kuba yarabiretse si umutima we ahubwo ni uko atabibonye.”

Icyo gihe ngo bituma iyo agarutse agasubira muri wa muryango yahozemo yisanga yabisubiyemo, niyo yaba yahawe icyo gukora, ari nabyo bibazo bikunze kugenda bigaragara ku basezererwa bakongera bakisanga bahagaruwe.

Is the artificial intelligence (AI) gold rush coming to an end, or is this simply a reality check?

That's the question which is hanging over investors, and which has prompted steep falls on the world's stock markets.

The sell-off in the US on Thursday was most dramatic on the Nasdaq, home to tech industry titans such as Alphabet, Nvidia, Meta and Apple.

It followed sweeping gains by the Democrats in this week's midterm elections in the US, which have given the party full control of Congress.

A number of leading Democrats campaigned against the unhindered expansion of data centres, which have underpinned the growth of artificial intelligence.

Fears this will lead to more regulation of AI appear to have concerned investors. But worries about the industry's prospects have been growing for some time.

The release of Chat GPT by Open AI in late 2022 is widely seen as having generated massive public and corporate interest in the practical uses of AI. It also sparked a modern-day gold rush.

Investors flocked to put their money into companies producing computer chips and networking infrastructure, building data centres and providing the energy to power them, as well as developing the AI itself. The value of tech companies soared.

The boom continued into this year. Investments in AI are expected to reach $1trillion in 2026 alone according to research by Goldman Sachs. The sector has scooped up so much available cash that other industries have seen their own borrowing costs increase as a result.

But investors want returns, and in recent months concerns have been growing about whether the AI boom can produce the expected riches.

Those worries have emerged at a time when public comments from AI researchers casting doubt over the safety of artificial intelligence - even suggesting it could represent an existential threat to humanity - have been grabbing headlines and fuelling speculation that a clampdown could lie ahead.

US tech stocks edge back up after AI slowdown fears sent value of firms plummeting

How does it affect me if share prices fall?

These firms you've never heard of are feeding fears the AI bubble could burst

While the Trump administration has been all-in on AI, or "super intelligence" as the president likes to call it, many leading Democrats tapped into grassroots concerns about the expansion of data centres and their impact on local communities.

These were largely focused on the facilities' high consumption of water and electricity, which many feared would push up their household bills – as well as the noise, use of land, and general disruption associated with them.

A Gallup poll published in May showed 71% of Americans would oppose the building of a data centre in their community. The figure for a nuclear power station was 53%.

James Talarico, who won the Senate race in once staunchly Republican Texas, was one of those to respond to this scepticism.

"While we want to protect America's leadership in artificial intelligence, we are still grappling with how it will affect everything from how we work to how our children learn," he said.

"We must protect Americans and establish clear, consistent laws for businesses."

With control of both houses of Congress, Democrats are now expected to challenge the president's technology agenda more vigorously, while introducing legislation which could curb the expansion of the industry.

Texas' Democratic governor-elect Gina Hinojosa campaigned against data centres, pledging a moratorium on the construction of new facilities.

Hinojosa's win could present opposition to tech multi-billionaire Elon Musk, who has moved large parts of SpaceX and Tesla's operations to the state, for years a Republican stronghold.

The Tesla boss had spent nearly $450m to back Republican campaigns in the midterms.

As the co-founder of the British-based technology firm Arm Holdings, Tudor Brown, points out, "stock values are based on future earnings not present earnings". If the rewards are not likely to be as great as expected, some investors will choose to sell up.

The falls seen on stock markets over the past 24 hours would appear to have been triggered by the midterm results. But concerns that tech firms have become overvalued were being expressed long before the elections.

The question now is whether this is simply the removal of froth from an over-exuberant market, or a sign that the AI rush is a bubble about to burst, with much wider consequences.

Nandini Roy Choudhury of Future Market Insights thinks investors will assess whether the political shift could result in restrictions on data centre construction, energy consumption and the deployment of AI technology.

She adds there is unlikely to be an immediate widespread recovery in tech stocks as traders are likely to be more selective, favouring firms with stronger balance sheets.

Brown thinks the impact will be limited. Share valuations, he thinks, were inflated by expectations of "almost infinite AI growth", which have been followed by "a bit of a panic".

"There is a natural floor to this", he says. "After that it will reflect I think that actually there's still a lot of money being made in these companies".

Last month's train crash in which 69 people died was the second deadly accident on the same high-speed line this year

European Union prosecutors have begun investigating the possible misuse of EU funds meant for upgrading the Spanish railway line where a train crash killed 69 people last week.

Prosecutors backed by a special unit of Spain's Guardia Civil security force said they were conducting the inquiry at the offices of Adif rail infrastructure authority and rail safety agency AESF.

The 28 October accident on the Madrid-Seville high-speed line was one of the worst railway disasters in Europe this century.

It is the second EU fraud inquiry opened into Spain's railways this year, after 46 people were killed on the same line at Adamuz in January.

Last week, a train operated by state-owned operator Renfe ploughed into the back of a stationary train belonging to private Spanish company Iryo outside the village of Urda, around 130km (80 miles) south of Madrid.

The LZB communication system that monitors the position of trains had gone down, and the Renfe train had been given the all clear to start running at normal speed, even though the Iryo train ahead of it had been unable to restart.

The two accidents nine months apart on the same line have claimed 115 lives and dozens more injuries.

Shock of rail tragedy gives way to sorrow and outrage in politically divided Spain

Spanish transport minister resigns days after deadly train crash

The European Public Prosecutor's Office (EPPO) said on Friday it had begun conducting investigative measures at Spain's rail authorities "after the opening of an investigation into possible fraud affecting EU funds , external allocated to the renovation and upgrading of safety, signalling and communications systems on the Madrid-Seville high-speed railway line".

The EPPO highlighted high public interest in the case, but said no further details would be made public.

As part of the process, a Spanish judge assigned to the case has to ensure the investigation complies with legal safeguards, including authorising any measures that might involve house searches or phone-tapping.

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez (C) faces parliamentary elections on 29 November

The Urda disaster has damaged the Socialist-led government of Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez ahead of a 29 November general election and the party is trailing the conservative People's Party (PP) in most opinion polls.

Close Sánchez ally Óscar Puente resigned this week as transport minister, after seeing two deadly accidents on his watch this year.

The PP and far-right Vox say Puente's resignation is not enough and they have demanded that Sánchez resign too.

Many people in Spain have now become wary of taking the train, with reports of widespread cancellations and empty station platforms.

A funeral for the 69 victims at Urda will take place on Tuesday at Toledo cathedral, in the same province that the disaster happened.

Puente's successor, Carlos Cuerpo, has vowed to take all necessary measures to "restore the confidence of Spaniards in our high-speed rail".

Cuerpo met survivors of January's Adamuz disaster on Friday and they handed him a list of 11 demands for improving safety on Spain's railways.

The naming of smoky bacon-flavoured crisps has become the latest political headache to emerge from the government's bid for closer ties with the EU.

The government is negotiating a deal on food standards in a bid to cut costs for British companies trading with Europe.

Labour ministers have been keen to talk up the potential economic benefits of the agreement, which could be announced at a summit later this month.

But the deal's requirement for Britain to adopt EU food rules in a wide range of areas has threatened to reignite sovereignty debates from the Brexit era.

Labour ministers have been keen to sidestep talking about the impact of alignment in particular sectors, instead stressing the overall economic boost it expects the food deal to bring.

On Thursday, Environment Secretary Angela Eagle told a radio presenter he should "get a life" when he asked about the potential impact of the new rules on snacks, such as smoky bacon crisps.

But it highlights the political dangers for the government of realigning with regulations that British politicians have not been able to shape, with the Conservatives and Reform UK keen to pounce on cases showing Britain to be a "rule taker" from Brussels.

It is not the first regulatory skirmish over smoky bacon crisps - following previous headlines over how the well-loved British flavour could be affected by an EU decision in 2024 to phase out a number of artificial smoke flavourings.

Now, the flavour name itself has been called into question by a separate EU attempt to restrict how descriptions of meat are used to market food.

Under rules adopted this summer, the EU plans to restrict the use of 31 terms, including bacon, drumstick and steak, to products that contain meat, claiming consumers could be confused by plant-based alternatives using the same names.

The European snack industry is seeking clarity on how the rules, which will also cover terms such as pork, chicken and beef, would apply to meat-flavoured crisps, including those flavoured without the use of any meat extracts.

The UK government has said it expects the new regulations to be in scope of its proposed food standards deal.

This means they would also apply to companies marketing their products in Britain, which is among the biggest consumers of crisps in Europe, according to analysts Euromonitor. , external

It has raised the prospect that crisps with names such as smoky bacon and roast chicken could have to be relabelled to be sold in British shops, although much remains unclear about how the rules will apply in practice.

The new EU rules, which will not come into force until after August 2029, will allow the European Commission to create exemptions for meaty names with an established long-term use to describe other types of food product.

The Brussels-based body is yet to set out how it plans to use this power, or what it means for snacks.

A group of conservative German MEPs are also seeking a specific carve-out for meat names in snacks and sauces in separate legislation , external currently making its way through the European Parliament.

The Food and Drink Federation, which represents British crispmakers including Walkers and KP Snacks, has been supportive of the government's bid to reach a food deal due to its potential to reduce trade barriers with Europe.

But it has highlighted the new rules as an example of where it wants the government to work with industry to ensure UK interests are reflected in EU decision making.

"Meat protections are an example of a new EU rule that UK businesses will need to comply with, but which the UK was not involved in developing," added the body's chief scientific officer Kate Halliwell.

The Potato Processors' Association, which also represents a number of major snackmakers, said it was monitoring the situation closely and wanted to see clarification of how the rules could affect its members.

Vanessa Richardson, its deputy director general, said her association supported moves to reduce "unnecessary barriers" in the trade of food products.

But she added it was important that the government's deal is implemented in a way that "avoids unintended consequences for established product descriptions which consumers clearly understand as referring to a flavour".

The Department for Environment, Food & Rural Affairs (Defra) says it stands ready to help British snack businesses prepare for the impact of the new EU rules.

It is not yet clear what a British version of the rules would look like, or whether they would need to apply from 2029 alongside the new European regulations.

Should under-16s be banned from buying energy drinks in Wales?

Young people and experts say they support the Welsh government's plan to ban children under-16 from buying high-caffeine energy drinks.

The Welsh government said that evidence suggests a link between "consumption of high-caffeine energy drinks and negative health outcomes", and was considering a ban on under-16s buying them.

BBC Wales spoke to young people in Cardiff who said they supported the proposed ban, with one 17-year-old saying it was "really easy to start relying on them".

The British Soft Drinks Association said the proposed ban was "unnecessary and not supported by robust evidence of overconsumption or harm".

The news follows the ban in England where drinks like Red Bull, Monster, Relentless and Prime will be illegal to sell to under-16s from April, aimed at reducing obesity levels, disrupted sleep and anxiety.

Any drink containing more than 150mg of caffeine per litre will be illegal to sell to children and younger teenagers in shops, restaurants, cafes, vending machines and online.

Lower-caffeine soft drinks, such Diet Coke, as well as tea and coffee are not affected.

Excessive caffeine consumption has been linked to headaches and sleep problems , and experts say young people can be more sensitive to caffeine as they have smaller bodies and their brains are still developing.

Some popular drinks brands contain more caffeine than two cups of coffee or four cans of cola.

Vee, 17, from Cardiff, said she was happy about the proposed ban, while Sunny, 16, urged people to "just have a coffee" instead of an energy drink.

Too much caffeine can cause a rapid heart rate, abnormal heart rhythms and seizures, and although rare, there have been some deaths linked to excess caffeine .

The sugary versions of the drinks can also contribute to obesity and damaged teeth, according to the Association of UK Dieticians.

Currently any drink, other than tea or coffee, with over 150mg requires a label warning of its high-caffeine content that says it is not recommended for children or pregnant or breast-feeding women.

For most adults, up to 400mg of caffeine a day, or about four cups of instant coffee or five cups of tea, is safe.

Sunny urged people to "just have a coffee" instead of an energy drink

Aisling Pigott, a nutritionist and registered dietician in Cardiff, said she was pleased to hear of the proposed ban but that it was probably "10 years too late".

She said Wales had "disproportionate concerns around diet and lifestyle" and while this would not be a "magic bullet", it was a "step in the right direction".

Pigott described caffeine as "a bit like going into your overdraft - you might immediately have a little bit more money or cash, but that does need to be repaid in some format".

She said someone may have a little more concentration, but that was "followed by a crash".

"Because I'm a dietitian, my concern around excessive consumption of these drinks also sits with what what are they not consuming when they're drinking?

"I see and hear a lot of children and young people drinking these drinks instead of food, so using the sugar and caffeine as an easier access to give energy than really nutritious, healthy, balanced diet."

Aisling Pigott says she was "so pleased to see this leadership coming from Wales"

In a written statement, Public and Preventative Health Minister Nerys Evans said the latest evidence suggested a link between consumption of high-caffeine energy drinks and negative health outcomes in children.

"This includes increased frequency of headaches, irritation, tiredness and stomach aches, reduced sleep duration and quality and increased risk of stress, anxiety and depression," she said.

"The previous Welsh government consulted and gathered evidence on proposals to restrict the sale of high-caffeine energy drinks to children under 16, with broad support for action."

Evans added: "Having considered the evidence and responses to that earlier consultation, the current Welsh government intends to take forward proposals to prohibit the sale of high-caffeine energy drinks to children under 16, subject to the outcome of this consultation.

"These are drinks, other than tea or coffee, that contain over 150mg of caffeine per litre."

The Welsh government said the consultation would seek views on the proposed "enforcement framework", including "online age-verification arrangements, assessing compliance activity, sanctions, implementation timescales and monitoring arrangements".

British Soft Drinks Association said its members had not marketed or promoted the sale of energy drinks to under-16s since 2010.

"All high-caffeine beverages carry a 'not recommended for children' label. The available evidence shows that the vast majority of caffeine consumed by children and adolescents comes from sources other than energy drinks."
